title: Emollients & soap substitutes
summary: Why emollients are the backbone of dry-skin and eczema care, how to choose between lotions, creams, gels and ointments, how much to prescribe, and the safety messages (fire risk, aqueous cream).

glance.think: Any dry or eczematous skin, at every review, alongside active treatment.
glance.engine: Emollients replace lipids and water in the stratum corneum, restore the barrier and reduce itch and flares.
glance.backbone: The right emollient is the one the patient will use: generous quantities (children 250–500 g a week), used as a soap substitute too; stop aqueous cream as a leave-on.
glance.never_miss: Fire risk with all emollients soaking into fabrics (MHRA); slips on bath additives; stinging from preservatives or aqueous cream.

what: Moisturisers that soften and hydrate the stratum corneum.

list: **Occlusives** (paraffins, petrolatum, dimeticone) reduce transepidermal water loss.
**Humectants** (urea, glycerol, lactic acid) draw water in.
**Emollient lipids** (ceramides, oils) fill gaps in the barrier.

what: Formulations range from light lotions/gels → creams → greasy ointments, which work best and contain the least preservative. They are used as **leave-on** treatments, as **soap substitutes**, and (now rarely) as bath additives.
features: Emollients restore the lipid "mortar" between corneocytes. They reduce water loss, irritant/allergen penetration and itch, and have a **steroid-sparing** effect (fewer flares, less steroid needed). In atopic eczema, filaggrin loss and soap/surfactant exposure drive barrier failure (see the [eczema](condition:eczema-dermatitis) notes see *Vitamin D analogues, coal tar*).
Step 0 of every eczema, psoriasis and ichthyosis plan. Also xerosis in older people, hand dermatitis and dryness after isotretinoin.

list: **"The best emollient is the one the patient will use."** Offer 2–4 to try (sample packs or self-selection, photo C03). Consider dryness, site, time of day, school/work, preference and **allergens/irritants**: avoid **fragrance**, and check for **lanolin** (wool alcohols), **SLS**, **methylisothiazolinone** and preservatives in creams.
**Quantity check:** NICE CG57 — **250–500 g/week** for children; about **500 g/week** for adults with widespread dryness. A patient collecting one 500 g tub every 3 months is under-using.
Prescribe enough for **home and nursery/school** (NICE CG57).

head: Product
Leave-on?
Teaching point
rows: Contains **sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS)** → stinging, burning, redness and measurable **barrier damage** (Danby 2011; MHRA 2013). At most a wash product; most formularies have dropped it
Oat protein — rare contact allergy; check the formulary (many ICBs restrict it)
Greasy ointment, also a soap substitute; **high fire risk** when soaked into fabric
Older versions contained SLS — switch if it stings

list: **Prescribe generously** (250–500 g/week for a child; ~500 g for an adult), in **pump dispensers** to reduce contamination, with a separate tub for the soap substitute.

**How to apply:** smooth on in the direction of hair growth (reduces folliculitis), often (at least 2–4 times daily and after washing), including when the skin is clear. Leave a gap between emollient and steroid.

**MHRA safety:** **Fire risk** with **both paraffin-containing and paraffin-free** emollients that dry onto clothing, bedding or dressings (DSU Dec 2018; reinforced 2020). Advise no smoking or naked flames; washing fabrics at high temperature may not remove all residue; tell carers and care homes; **Slips** in the bath/shower with emollient bath additives. Bath additives add no benefit (BATHE trial), and NICE CG57 (updated 2023) no longer advises offering them routinely
**Aqueous cream** (MHRA DSU 2013): may irritate the skin, particularly in children with eczema, probably because of SLS.
Eczema still uncontrolled despite adequate emollient + TCS (see NICE CG57 referral criteria); suspected emollient contact allergy (patch testing); erythroderma; infection.
Fully within community/primary-care IP and OTC practice. Follow ICB self-care/formulary policies; many ICBs expect OTC purchase for mild dry skin.

red_flags: Warn about **fire risk**: dressings, clothing and bedding soaked in any emollient (paraffin or paraffin-free) can catch fire easily (MHRA).
pearls: "Emollients are the treatment, not an extra."
Show the FTU *and* a handful of emollient. For a child with widespread eczema, a 500 g tub should last about a week.
Fire-safety counselling is an MHRA expectation — record that you gave it.
